newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries ending in tight ranges ahead of data.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries ending in tight ranges ahead of data.

text.p: The prices of U.S. Treasury securities were closing in tight ranges on Friday as market participants looked forward to a bevy of economic releases next week.

Durable goods orders and existing home sales data were released on Friday, but neither figure had much impact on the prices of bonds. Instead, investors were more concerned with the upcoming Employment Cost Index for the second quarter scheduled for release on Tuesday and the July nonfarm payrolls report set for release on Friday.

Activity slowed to a virtual crawl at about noon in New York as many players left to start an early summer weekend. With no data due there was little incentive to remain by trading screens, participants said.

"It was a tight range, but it's been an impressive day for bonds," said Hugh Johnson, chief economist at First Albany Corp. He said the market saw reassuring news in the drop of existing home sales -- down 2.6 percent to an annualized rate of 4.14 million -- and managed to avoid much damage in the strong durable goods orders report. Orders rose 2.3 percent in June, the biggest jump since January.
Johnson said nondefense capital goods -- up 2.1 percent -- was a particularly impressive number as it served as a leading indicator on the economy.
"The good news is how the bond market has remained relatively stable despite the strong durable goods number," Johnson said.

Treasuries continued to benefit from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's upbeat reading on the U.S. economy, Johnson said. They also were supported by the continued strength seen in the dollar, a trend that has sparked strong foreign purchases in Treasuries, he said.
"We remain in the mode we've been in, a grinding rally to higher prices and lower yields," said John Ryding, senior economist at Bear Stearns & Co Inc.

Ryding saw inflation as remaining contained and predicted more holders of mortgage-backed securities would swap into Treasury securities next week as the yield on the 10-year Treasury note flirted at falling to 6.10 percent.
"It gets progressively more painful as we get close to 6.10 percent on the 10-year," he said.
The market also had to absorb the GDP numbers next week, but Ryding saw a continuation of recent trends.

The Treasury's 30-year bond was closing down 4/32 at 102-10/32 to yield 6.45 percent. Three-month bills were one basis point higher at 5.09 percent. Six-month bills were up one basis point at 5.14 percent and year bills were up one basis point at 5.23 percent.

The 10-year issue was down 3/32 at 103-9/32 to yield 6.17 percent. The five-year note was off 1/32 at 99-22/32 yielding 6.07 percent. The two-year note was down 1/32 at 100-even to yield 5.88 percent.
